title: National Petroleum Refiners Association v. FTC (1973)
shortTitle: National Petroleum Refiners Association v. FTC (1973)
summary: The D.C. Circuit construed the FTC Act’s general rulemaking clause to authorize substantive rules elaborating the Act’s unfairness and deception standards.
notes: Judge J. Skelly Wright wrote for the panel (482 F.2d 672), certiorari was denied in 1974, and Congress responded in the 1975 Magnuson-Moss Act by expressly confirming FTC rulemaking authority while imposing special hybrid procedures on it.

sections.Parties: Two trade associations and thirty-four gasoline refining companies challenged an FTC trade regulation rule. The Commission defended its power to issue substantive standards under § 6(g) of the FTC Act.
sections.Material Facts: The rule classified failure to disclose gasoline octane ratings conspicuously on covered retail pumps as an unfair method of competition and an unfair or deceptive act or practice. In later enforcement, the FTC would still have to issue a complaint, hold a hearing, make findings, and obtain a cease-and-desist order, but it would not need to relitigate the rule’s general premise that the omission was unlawful. Plaintiffs argued that § 5’s detailed adjudication mechanism displaced substantive rulemaking and that § 6(g) authorized only procedural or housekeeping rules.
sections.Procedural History: The district court decided the case solely on statutory authority and held that the FTC lacked power to issue such substantive rules. The D.C. Circuit reversed and remanded for further proceedings. The decision therefore resolved authority rather than every objection to the octane rule.
sections.Issue: Did § 6(g), read with § 5’s enforcement provisions, authorize binding substantive rules elaborating the statutory standards, or only internal procedural rules?
sections.Holding: The court held that the FTC could promulgate substantive rules defining the statutory illegality it was empowered to prevent. The agency retained the obligation to use the specified adjudicatory enforcement process against individual offenders.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with the broad authorization to make rules and regulations for carrying out the Act and found no exclusive language in § 5. Rules could make adjudication more efficient by fixing recurring legal and factual premises in advance. Decisions involving other agencies supported reading general rulemaking grants to permit substantive standards. The court also emphasized notice, wider participation, consistent treatment of competitors, and fewer opportunities to profit from enforcement delay.

The court treated legislative history as ambiguous and earlier agency disclaimers as nonconclusive on a legal interpretation requiring judicial judgment. Later specific grants of rulemaking could reflect caution or a desire to settle uncertainty rather than prove that the original grant was absent. At the same time, it acknowledged statutory limits and judicial review of the legal standard and the rule’s reasons. The following notes question how its functional reasoning fits later textual and major-questions approaches and explain subsequent FTC legislation; this historical holding does not itself resolve every modern claim of FTC authority.

topics.lrs-o-rulemaking-authority: The D.C. Circuit construed § 6(g) and the statutory scheme as authorizing substantive rules specifying unfair or deceptive practices.
topics.lrs-s-enabling-statute: The whole dispute is whether the FTC's enabling statute, read as a whole, is a source of substantive rulemaking power.
